newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Parliament speaker misses sparring in low-key campaign.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Parliament speaker misses sparring in low-key campaign.

text.p: As the speaker of the House of Commons and with no serious opposition, Betty Boothroyd's re-election is the only certainty in Britain's election on Thursday.
In 1992 she won the seat of West Bromwich West for the opposition Labour Party with a majority of nearly 8,000. This time she has the backing of Labour and all the main parties.
But the first woman speaker in the 600-year history of parliament is still taking no chances.
She has hit the campaign trail in the blue collar constituency in the English Midlands with characteristic gusto.

"Order, Order," she bellowed, mimicking her no-nonsense performance in parliament as factory workers in this industrial town on the outskirts of Birmingham chatted while waiting for her to unveil a plaque.
Boothroyd is a matronly woman who has charmed the nation. Opinion polls indicate the former dancer would be a popular head of state if Britain were to become a republic.

In parliament, in her sombre black and gold robe and buckled shoes, the 67-year-old Boothroyd is referred to as "Madam Speaker", but to the people she has served as an MP since she was first elected in 1973 she is simply "Our Betty".

Forty years ago, Boothroyd's return as speaker would have been automatic, but that tradition was changed in the 1960s. She renounced her Labour affiliation in 1992, when she was elected speaker, to be impartial.
But her popularity has ensured that convention has been ignored in West Bromwich.
She is backed by the ruling Conservatives, the Labour party and the minority Liberal Democrats and her only opponents are from two minor fringe parties.
NON-POLITICAL CAMPAIGN
In line with her role as speaker her election campaign is completely non-political. She eschews the red of Labour for a neutral green, the colour of parliament, in her campaign.
"It's difficult. This is my 12th election campaign and it is probably the most difficult," she told Reuters. "I'm no longer a political animal. I've had to step aside from politics."
Boothroyd's is one of only two seats in the country where all the major political parties are not fielding candidates.
In the other, former BBC journalist Martin Bell is running as an independent against Conservative ex-minister Neil Hamilton who is embroiled in a sleaze scandal.
Free of the pressure of campaigning, Boothroyd was obviously in her element and thoroughly enjoying herself. She planned a full programme in the final days before the election.
"I voted for her," said George Roper, a 50-year-old factory worker. He thought she was a great speaker of the house.
"She sorts them lot out. She's doing a great job there."
His co-worker Mike Stackhouse agreed. "She's got that female ability of controlling people. We could do with more women in parliament. I wouldn't be a bad thing," he said.
Stackhouse and Roper, like most Britons, have seen Boothroyd take command of the often rowdy members of parliament thanks to the introduction of television cameras in 1989.
Boothroyd says the best description of her job as speaker has been likened to a "cross between a school mistress and a nanny".
Despite what often seems a difficult job -- keeping the predominately male parliament in order during emotional and heated debates -- she says it can be fun.
"I enjoy it. "I give them so much rope and then..." she laughed.

She issued a severe reprimand to Labour Party leader Tony Blair when he called Prime Minister John Major a 'dimwit' in a parliamentary exchange. But she has allowed terms such as humbug and fathead to get through.
Boothroyd attributes her popularity in parliament and in her constituency in the cradle of the industrial revolution to her sense of humour.
"I can laugh at people and at myself," she said.
Douglas Parish, Boothroyd's campaign agent, thinks her success is at least partly due to her humble beginnings as the only daughter of a mill worker in Yorkshire.
"She comes from a similar sort of area. This is an industrial working class area. She has an affinity for the people and they have an affinity for her."
Before joining parliament, Boothroyd honed her political skills working for Labour members of parliament and during a stint in the Foreign Office.
In the 1960s she helped in former president John Kennedy's campaign and worked as an aide to a U.S. congressman.
Although she never married, there seems to have been no shortage of suitors. Politics and parliament seem to be the loves of her life.
"I'm used to the cut and thrust of politics," said Boothroyd as she resumed her campaign. "But I'm managing."
